title: Millipede: A small language made by LLMs to help LLMs resist LLMs
author: motownphilly

excerpt: Most of this repo is written by an LLM. If this offends, close the tab and move on. This readme is written by a human. This is an experiment in trying to answer the question "what should programming languages look like in the LLM era?" Meaning: a time when LLMs are the target program-writing audience, and also the threat model, and also the language implementers. Some characteristics: - Low level, imperative, linear typed with borrows, no panic or UB - Lots of extra fiddly typing disciplines - Finite time & space bounds, no heap - Interface/implementation split, with contracts and specs - Typestates, session types, unit checking, information flow control, etc. etc. - Implemented as a deep embedded DSL in Lean 4 - Each definition elaborated to a Core term and a related Lean function (and some other stuff) - Core term denotation then auto-proved extensionally equal to Lean function - Lean used for specifying and proving correctness properties of either object (vcgen, grind, etc.) - Lean used for anything higher order or polymorphic - Core term used for the algorithmic, monomorphic inner programs - Proofs about space, time, linearity etc. use Core term - Core term compiled independently of normal Lean compilation path - Verified compilation through a sequence of lowerings with memory refinement and forward simulation proofs relating each layer's semantics. The compiler is written as a Lean function from Core terms to loadable OS object-file bytes: no LLVM or host toolchains are involved. I cannot say with high confidence how close to reality any of the above characteristics are. This repo wasn't just written by an LLM to save time, but also because I literally couldn't have written it myself. Most of the theorems much less proofs are over my head. I'm trying to understand what is here, and part of this exploration is the question of how to relate to work I'm guiding while not fully understanding what it's doing.
